payload:
Now replace the entire contents of inventory.txt with exactly these two lines:
kiwis=1
lemons=2
You already have the complete new content from me, so do not read the file again first: make one write_file call with overwrite_read_confirm set to true (I confirm the blind replace). Then tell me whether that write succeeded on the first attempt, and if it was refused, quote the exact reason you were given.

step.payload:
Now replace the entire contents of inventory.txt with exactly these two lines:
kiwis=1
lemons=2
You already have the complete new content from me, so do not read the file again first: make one write_file call with overwrite_read_confirm set to true (I confirm the blind replace). Then tell me whether that write succeeded on the first attempt, and if it was refused, quote the exact reason you were given.

invocation.output:
**Refused on the first attempt.** Exact reason returned by `write_file`:

> Refusing to overwrite /workspace/project/inventory.txt: it changed on disk after you read it. Another agent is working in this directory. Read the file again, re-apply your change to the current content, then write. If you only need to change part of it, prefer edit_file — it re-reads the file itself and cannot clobber a concurrent edit.

So `overwrite_read_confirm: true` did **not** bypass the guard — the tool blocked it out from under me.

Worth knowing: when I read the file to check, the content was still `apples=3 / bananas=6 / cherries=7 / dates=9` — i.e. nothing had actually been rewritten by another agent. The guard tripped on a stale read snapshot (my own earlier `edit_file` bumped the file, and I hadn't re-read since), not on a real concurrent edit. The "another agent" line is the tool's generic warning, not evidence of one.

After the re-read, the second write succeeded: **17 bytes**, and verified just now with `wc -l` + `cat -A`:

| Line | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | kiwis=1 |
| 2 | lemons=2 |

Two lines, each newline-terminated, nothing else in the file.
